text:
When the appliance, its cables, plugs, and connections are in perfect condition, an inferior or reduced voltage from the mains can still cause them to increase in heat. For example, the Nvidia 5090 cable, plug and conectors. Here's why:

When voltage drops, the appliance compensates by drawing more current to maintain its required power output (as per \( P = V \times I \), where \( P \) is power, \( V \) is voltage, and \( I \) is current). This higher current generates more heat in the cables and connections due to the inherent electrical resistance in the wires, according to Joule's law (\( \text{Heat} = I^2R \), where \( I \) is current and \( R \) is resistance). This increased heat can become noticeable even if everything is functioning as intended. 

It's one of the reasons why stable voltage supply and proper circuit design are so essential in preventing overheating and ensuring safety. Would you like help exploring practical ways to address voltage drops or cable ratings?

text:
But like, genuinely guys, why are we even excited? It's like I'm happy for all the tech-tubers getting their hands on it, but like:

1. We'll never get our hands on one, not until 2-3 gens pass anyway, then maybe.

2. Even if you did, you would never be able to afford it.

3. By the time you get your hands on one, like I said, multiple gens have passed, so are you even excited?

4. I'm not going to start the whole "AI is bad" debate here, but it's mostly fake frames so there is no improvement really, we're basically celebrating being able to be fooled by AI at this point. It isn't even better than last gen, we are genuinely hyping a product costing more than last time all the while literally never getting to try it ourselves, that's it, that's literally the entire video, what are we doing here?

I'm not trying to be a hater but I just don't understand the hype anymore, like what exactly are you hyping as a potential buyer? Getting the card in 10 years? Or "Ooh look at that performance I wish I had, cool tech, too bad I can't have it!" Isn't the whole point of GPU reviews to see what you want to have or are planning to buy? Take that out of the equation and what are you left with? It's literally, "Hm... More FPS than last year... Cool... Anyway..."

Please understand, I'm NOT hating on LTT, I love this channel and I'm here for the entertainment, and sure I guess that answers my question above as to why others are here too, but I'm more speaking about the people unironically hyped about the card. Like my man, you will NOT have it nor can you afford it, what exactly is it that you hype? I genuinely don't understand, PC has reached a point where we are basically people in poverty hyping the next Lamborghini release, like how does that affect your life exactly? What is the hype about? But it's worse still, this is fake frames and AI, so that's like Lamborghini saying, "Oh this car isn't faster, it's the same speed as last year, but the windshield has AI tech to make the environment around you SEEM like it's going by faster so the car FEELS faster but isn't really. Anyway the tech makes the price double." It's like you can't even hype that as an enthusiast, there are no improvements to the car or engine or brand, it's nothing but costs you more for the sake of money for them, not you.

So once more, what exactly are YOU the consumer hyping up in this instance, be honest. I just genuinely don't understand the hype around GPU releases anymore, the very BUYING part has been deleted from the entire ordeal, so we are hyping seeing something unfold on screen? At that point we might as well fake a review from 2099 about the ZTX 9099Ti with 10 billion AI frames y'all! Since you'll never get to experience that card yourself, the end result is the same, you're just watching a YouTube tech demo of stuff that is effectively not real to you since you cannot have it.

text: I want there to be an option that makes shaders bake the shadows into a layer that is applied directly to the texture and only recalculate shadows when I'm hitting the fps limit.  The only shadow I really need in realtime is my player's shadow, and even then I could handle it updating every other frame as long as all the polygons in the frame update every frame.  Without shaders most games would run really fast since rasterization is really well optimized.  I purpose a list of objects and how long its been since their shadowmap was updated, then with the time left between frames the card can work through the list and update the oldest shadowmaps first.  This way you always bounce off the frame limit.

text:
For a GPU to render/draw the "3 Fake Frames in between", it must already know what the "Next Real Frame" looks like.
This is the real issue!
So for a Game being Faked into 4x fps, the GPU has to hold back the next frame that it already knows about to be able to draw the next 3 fake frames.
Consider 6fps raw, 1/60th of a second it holds that next frame back, it is adding 16.66 ms of latency to every rendered frame.

This would easily be seen on camera. Why is no one demonstrating this!
author: @NZTechArc

text: CNNs are faster / more efficient than transformers, partly due to locality bias. The "scaling" Nvidia mentions is that transformers get better with more parameters / training in a way that CNNs don't. So the transformer is likely larger than the CNN, making it even more impressive that they are able to run in real time.

text: I think the simplest way to explain convolutional neural networks is: for every pixel, a new pixel value is calculated based on its nearby neighbours. E.g. if every pixel is replaced with the average of its neighbours, you get a blur effect. Think of a visual illusion where you see some broken lines and your mind fills in the missing parts of the line, that's how these CNNs would be used to preserve detail as they upscale. However, it's a lot of computation, and a challenge to preserve scene integrity because the neighbourhoods are small compared to the entire scene. Transformer models allow arbitrary areas to serve as context when computing new pixel values; think of it as like having configurable neighbourhoods to input to that computation. E.g. when trying to upscale the left side of a road in the game's scene, that computation can also refer to the right side of the road all the way across the screen.

text: One way to explain the tensor cores and neural shading is as follows: The neural networks can be used to approximate extremely complicated functions for which we can't just write simple equations. However, we can create those networks with a simple procedure merely by showing them many examples. So for example we can show it what rocky terrain looks like at all levels of detail, and the network will learn how to do that, using less data (just what the network's values are) than trying to store all the terrain (what the network computes as output). It's sort of like procedural terrain, but learned instead of programmed. The tensor cores are what are used to efficiently compute those trained neural networks on the GPU. They're not the same as geometry or pixel shaders, so they need their own specialized cores for the task.

text: The 50 series is a huge letdown. They're good cards of course, but the way Nvidia talks about this stuff, you always expect a revolution, and you get an evolution. These are 40 series cards with a crapload of power pumped into them to keep stable. This is not exactly ideal. Nvidia is way too distracted with side projects. They've got 5000 features they're working on, and only a small handful of them ever pan out. Don't get me wrong, I love Nvidia. If it weren't for them, we'd be in a world of hurt. However, when it comes to just raw 3d rendering, we're getting screwed. I bought a GTX1080 for $500 in 2017, and today that will buy me a 4070. The 4070S is another $120. 8 years and only 85% improvement. That's insane. There was almost the same improvement from the 900 series to the 10 series, and that was 2 years. People always ask me "dude how can you still run a GTX1080 and a 7700k?!?!" and it's because I have a Gsync 144hz display, and in competitive games we all turn down graphics settings so I get lots of frames, and in games that aren't competitive, I have Gsync. So really nothing will change yet. Not until I can afford a card that will drive 1440p at 240hz+ for affordable prices. I'm not paying a thousand dollars for a graphics card. I have other hobbies.

text:
6:50 Professional "AI Dork" here... The 5090 having 32GB VRAM is basically useless. It will not be able to run hardly anything that the 4090 can't already run blisteringly fast

For example, my 3090 can generate text with a maximum size model that can fit in 24GB VRAM at over 120 words per second across 4 streams, which is already monumentally faster than any normal person can read

Now, the 5090 can fit damn near no bigger models (cause 32GB VRAM is still pitifully small for LLMs, not even being able to fit a full precision 20B param model when we have models that are 600B-1T+ in size now), but at an even faster speed, which basically nobody wants. The limit of quality for local AI is not speed. It hasn't been for a very long time. The limit is quality and network size, something of which the 5090 will do basically nothing to improve.

So in essence, you can't really run anything too much better on the 5090, and now instead of generating at 3x the speed you can read, you can gen at 4x the speed you can read... groundbreaking

So yeah, the 32GB VRAM for the 5090 is the absolute bare minimum they could have given, and will still be a severe artificial limit on how useful the 5090 will ever be. A 3 gen old original A6000, which is like 1/5th the speed of the 5090 is far more useful, simply for the fact it has 48GB VRAM. People want better quality, not more speed when you are already way faster than you need to be

In reality, you use more symbols for a more efficient encoding - 7 trits to 11 bits.

text:
Isn't the latency measurement flawed? It's really strange that the FG didn't increase the latency unless Reflex 2 wasn't enabled. Is LDAT picking up changes between generated frames as the end of the latency test?
I mean, if comparing apple to apple, meaning everything identical except for frame gen being enabled (especially with reflex 1 enabled in both cases), there is no way that FG would be the same or better then no FG.
I mean, FG works by waiting for a frame to be rendered in order to generate interpolated frames BEFORE that last rendered frame (not predicting the future but simply interpolating between 2 rendered frames). It basically means you're displaying 1 rendered frame late compared to no FG (the last rendered frame with the latest inputs is not displayed as soon as it is ready, but is first used for generating the "fake" ones which are displayed first). 
That makes it impossible for the latency to be the same of better, unless Reflex 2 is enabled and its asynchronous reprojection mechanism kind of propagate the user action into the generated frames (movements could be simulated but animations and network action wouldn't).

text:
When Nvidia is chalking out a new product range, there is a maximum die size that they can produce cost effectively at scale. Assuming Moore's law is mostly trucking along, it's around 600mm2 and 40% faster than last gen. For this example, lets say a new generation die is 600mm2 and has 10,000 cores and is given the nomenclature EX-102 (102 notates that highest end non data center silicon)

The tradition would then follow that their Titan and Quadro cards would get 95%-100% of the number of cores that this full 102 die has to offer (because they are using this die). So in this example they would have 10,000 cores.

The 80ti - Also on a 102 - 93% of the 10,000 cores, so around 9300 cores.

The 80 - 102/103 - 66-80% of the 102's full cores. But here's the thing. Sometimes these end up on 103. A smaller, cheaper, die. The other skus up until this point have fused off sections of the 102 die. The 103 is a different piece of silicon entirely. While it might seem unfair to compare them, they are still the same in architecture and scale linearly in some workloads. In any case, we would expect 66% of the cores or in this example 6600 cuda cores.

The 70 class cards are normally 50% and built on 104 so 5000 cores

The 60 class on 106 and hovers around the low 30s or 3000 cores

-----------------------------------------------

This is the expectation as it has been set for the better part of 15 years. It has only been until last gen [4000 series] that we received cards that were substantially different.

The last 90 sku was 87% of the full 102 die. Substantially less than a normal 80ti or titan but curiously, significantly more money. The 80ti, which used to give you the most silicon for the money (again around 90%) is now gone and replaced with the 4080 super, which was 55%. A noticeable drop in the amount of silicon. The standard 4080 even worse at 52%. The 4070 is a shocking 32%.

Using the data I've listed above, it is clear to see that Nvidia has merely moved their entire stack down to make room for their 90 class cards. Again... these 90 cards have no substantial architecture differences that justifies the creation of a new sku. They aren't substantially more silicon. No HBM. No MCM. No stacked cache. They are just an 80ti class with 2-3gb vram modules soldered on. Is that worth $1500-$2000? Maybe... But what I cannot abide by is the squashing of the rest of their product stack to make it look like a better value than it really is.

Now we have the release of the 50 series.

5090 - 102 - 88% of 102 cores
5080 - 103 - 45%
5070 - 104 - 31 %

Are you seeing the downward pattern here? In two generations we have seen 80 class cards go from 80% of all the possible cores (3000 series) to 45% and increase from $699 to $999. Even adjusted for inflation, there is a massive markup on this.

I've really gone on long enough and bless you to anyone who has taken the time to read this.

text:
10:55 I'm sorry but this is false. CNNs are far superior to transformers in terms of performance and efficiency. Attention (the driving force behind transformers) even with super-optimized libraries such as flash-attention2 are always slower than convolutions (theoretically in time complexity as well) - we also have really fast ways of computing convolutions (spoiler: using FFTs !). 

I am very disappointed that this is the way our research has led us to, where it is essentially "bigger model better" with a stupid architecture like transformers rather than having a better thought out architecture and task-specific models. Although there is good research being done on replacing attention once and for all. Long convolutions are a promising line of work: with sublinear complexity and a "information heavy" architecture similar to the attention operator.

Kena 50s 3060, 3070 80s 1440p

New world 1440p 3060 70s, 3070 100

Flight sim 1440p, 3060 40s, 3070 60s

Forza 3070 4k 100,3080 130 on average 

Hitman 3070 60s 4k, 3080 80s

4060 4K tsunama at 25 fps, 4070 40s no DLSS 

Elden Ring no DLSS 1440p, 4060 40 fps, 4070 70
 
 
  4080 Forza 4080 110 fps, 4080 140 4K

Avatar 4k 50fps 4080, 4090 70

Hogwarts 4080 4k 45s, 60 4090
 
As you guys can see, I compared models directly under a higher class, as that's the only way it makes a higher class worth it since the jump will be bigger, which is why it makes no sense to compare a 4090 to a 5090 only 1 gen apart. It only makes sense to compare the 4080 to the 5090, which will skip the 4080s; this way it shows a good jump. The same goes for coming from a card like mine, 4070, to the 5080 or 4060 to 5070.

text:
@manofnetliveson  It has to do with the electrical resistance of copper at such microscopic scales. To quote Griselda Bonilla, senior manager of advanced BEOL interconnect technology research at IBM. “As dimensions shrink, the line resistance increases disproportionately, accounting for a higher fraction of the total delay. The resistance increase is driven by several factors, including reduced conductor cross-section, further-reduced volume fraction of copper due to non-scaled high-resistivity barriers and liner layers, and added resistivity due to lossy electron scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries.”

TLDR: Physics are limiting us going any smaller. And there isn't any new tech that is ready for production.

text:
@ashleybarnes9343  how much is that contributing to the increase in performance over the 4090? If we are seeing 30% performance with 33% more cores, roughly as much more power consumed, how much of the performance improvement can you really attribute to faster VRAM?

Yes, the GDDR7 VRAM is faster than GDDR6X, and the 5090 with GDDR7 technically has 79% more memory bandwidth than the GDDR6X on the 4090, but looking at the widely reported average performance improvements over the 4090 given that the 5090 has roughly the same percentage increase in additional GPU processing power, can you honestly say that you'd be confident stating that if the 4090 Ti was released with the same 33% increase in GPU cores but GDDR6X that you wouldn't expect similar performance uplift over the 4090 that we see here with the 5090?

I'm saying it's far more likely that the increase in GPU cores amounts to 90% of the uplift, and the GDDR7 VRAM maybe 10%.

That's not to say that GDDR7 doesn't provide other improvements not typically critical metrics measured by gaming and enthusiast media reviewers, maybe GDDR7 also provides a meaningful reduction in frame to frame time latency under specific load conditions or resolutions, or, that additional bandwidth is what allows 4X frame generation to work with acceptable latencies or accuracy. Anyway, a month later and I'm even more disappointed.

text:
The AI benchmarks were kinda useless to us looking for such. UL Procyon is kinda only representative of a narrow scope of lite duty usage on Windows. The only bit I can semi-confidently infer from these charts is that we are maybe looking at somewhere above a 20% increase and the only (relative) high gains NV claimed are going to be seen almost entirely from the FP4 support.

For LLM inference at FP4, that could be big. For anything else, right now it looks like it down to cost-performance and the additional VRAM.

Right now, I'm around as disappointed as I expected with the bulk of the improvement only seen at FP4.

For reference, image gen at FP4 has a very significant quality and prompt adherence penalty. The are mainly two reason to choose to run an image gen model a that low of a quantization: not enough VRAM to run the model at FP16 or even FP8, or to make benchmark numbers higher, ie. not caring about the actual output.

The issue, is that at 72hz, it runs very poorly, and it's just not usable (36hz to 72hz)

But at 120hz (60hz), it starts being usable, sometimes.
The same goes for 144hz (72hz)...

The issue? It doesn't matter if your headset runs at 120 or 144hz, because 60+ FPS will be reasonable, and even better than using "frame gen", so it's a straight up useless technology, no matter what you do, because when the game is not playable, it sucks, but when it starts making sense, you can run the game just fine without it...

You forgot to mention your main sponsor, Nvidia, lmao... I mean, you tested input latency, and it was somehow, magically lower than with MFG disabled? Why present the error, and not the actual correct results?

MFG HAS to add latency, it's physically IMPOSSIBLE for it to NOT add latency, because4 the way MFG works, is that it HOLDS 2 frames, until it can generate 3 frames in between them... Going from "Sample - hold - sample - hold" which is what normal GPU's do, to "hold - sample - hold - hold - sample - hold - hold - sample - hold" is a significantly longer process... Reflex can only MINIMIZE the time this process takes, it can not remove it.

Every test from other sources of 40-series cards doing framegen shows appropriate increase in latency, but you guys go ahead, and add the obviously flawed results in your video? text:
I love that we're going back to the GTX 280 with a big die, and an even bigger 512 bit memory bus
Too bad its $2000, still a great card.


20:50 Of note, the 4090 saw a greater uplift over the 30 series because it is the only card in class parity with the previous generation
The 4090 and 3090/TI are all ~600mm 384 bit bus
Compare the rest of the 40 series to the 30 series and you'll see that the 16GB 4080 is basically a 4nm version of the 3070/TI with double the RAM but both cards being ~400mm 256 bit memory bus
The 12GB 4080? Effectively a 4nm version of the 12GB 3060 but with GDDR6X and a huge overclock with both cards being ~300mm on a 192 bit bus
Oh, and the closest card in the class of the 4060TI is the old GTX 1650 Super ( the small form factor version without 6 pin power had special place in my heart for adding new life to office PCs) both of these cards are ~200mm with a 128 bit memory bus.

text: The lower latency with dlss is not that surprising to me. The AI assisted MFG is not based on native screen space frame information, it uses data from the rendering pipeline before the native frame is completely calculated. You can even improve some of these pipeline stages with AI, allowing for faster native frame calculation, though this would further convolute the discussion. Then, with some thread optimizations you can end up with higher fps and lower latency. Not so surprising to me.

text:
15:30 those are most likely accurate measurements. Reflex fast-tracks human input to gpu frames and makes predictions in the image. Now add frame gen with it, which also predicts the future (it does NOT blend past frames), and you see the predictions made by reflex sooner. To try to illustrate, here's a list of frames with MFG 3x:

1 ---REAL FRAME (player clicks mouse)
2 predicted frame
3 predicted frame (soonest mouse click is rendered with reflex and frame gen)
4 ---REAL FRAME (soonest mouse click is rendered with reflex and no frame gen)
5 predicted frame
6 predicted frame
7 ---REAL FRAME (soonest mouse click is rendered with no reflex and no frame gen)
8 predicted frame
9 predicted frame

text:
Casualmente son las mismas conclusiones a las que llegué luego de probar la GPU en el CES y que detalle a fondo en mi video de PC NOTICIAS: "No compres una RTX 50 sin antes ver este video"

Veamos:

-La 5090 es la GPU más potente de escritorio que existe hoy por hoy, sin discusión, tanto a nivel de rasterizado como a nivel de Ray tracing

-La 5090 es la GPU de escrito que más consume, sin discusión, en juegos llega a consumir más de 560W, eso es más de 100W por encima de la 4090

-La diferencia de rendimiento entre la 5090 a la 4090 es mucho más pequeña que de la 4090 a la 3090, es decir: hubo un salto más grande de potencia de la 4090 vs la 3090, que de la 5090 vs 4090

-La 5090 queda entre las tarjetas con relación precio/ desempeño menos favorable. Es la más potente y exclusiva y la exclusividad se paga

-La 5090 presenta las latencias más bajas al jugar usando reescalado (menos de 30ms) pero son las más altas al activar el multi frame generation (más de 50 ms)

-El reflex 2 para bajar latencias solamente estará disponible de momento en dos juegos, tocará esperar a que se implemente en más juegos y ver si vale la pena jugar con el MFG sin que el juego se sienta muy laggeado.

text:
I just upgraded to a 1440p 360hz OLED monitor, and 4k 240 is pretty common on the market now as well. I feel like the best advantage that frame gen offers is to set a target base frame rate of ~60 hz and add frames to take advantage of these incredibly fast new monitors. 60 will be more than playable latency for story games, and the added perceived motion smoothness (especially on OLED) will probably be worth the little bit of artifacting. Hopefully this is especially true since DLSS4 is supposed to have less impact on base frame rate.

I understand the argument that they are fake frames, but I do believe that neural rendering is going to be a big part of future graphical improvements as we see the raw performance gains from new process nodes being smaller and less frequent, especially on a per dollar basis. There have been a lot of cool papers in the past 5-10 years, many from Nvidia but not all, that showcase using learning techniques and other statistical approaches to do some really visually impressive stuff. At the end of the day the human eye is very easily tricked. So long as temporal coherence is maintained and visual artifacts are small and move slowly, it will all look very convincing.

All in all I am excited for this tech to work it's way down the product stack too a more affordable price as I believe the lower end cards have more to gain from technology like DLSS

text:
This is such a strange GPU launch. I love the cooler and hardware design - I wouldn't call it revolutionary (as I don't expect to see it widely adopted), but it's definitely a real innovation, and impressively dense in both board and cooler design. But then the performance is ... meh? For the price, two and a half years later? Unimpressive. DLSS 4 seems pretty cool, but it's also more of the same - nobody needs 200fps in Cyberpunk, and it's useless for games that really need high frame rates, so it's really much more useful for lower end hardware than this - though I for one don't want to be playing something graphically intensive at 15fps-quadrupled-to-60 on a 5060 either, given the input lag. I'm firmly in the pro-upscaling camp, and this is a definite advancement, but not necessarily all in the direction we actually need. So ... eh? I did spend almost this much on my last GPU during the pandemic, but I'm definitely not doing that again, so luckily I'm not in the market for something like this.

Oh, and I'm disappointed to see LTT adopt AI slop generation benchmarks. I'm all for benchmarking AI performance in use cases that are actually useful (not to mention legal!), but image generation is a silly toy at best, and mass scale copyright infringement burning much needed energy for no purpose beyond endangering the jobs of already vulnerable artists, illustrators and designers at worst. That's one type of benchmark I'd be happy to see you skip going forward.

text: 11:00 I very much appreciate you trying to disentagle the buzz-words and explaining CNNs and Transformers. The issue I have is that Transformers actually have a slower inference time at the same quality compared to CNNs, which is why for real-time stuff CNNs still dominate. So I find that argument very confusing. If I had to guess I'd say they managed to squeeze out more quality out of the transformer model by using significantly more data. They tend to require way more training data but scale better with it if you have a lot. But honestly, I think the difference between CNNs and Transformers is almost irrelevant here. I'm pretty sure they could've made either work and Transformers just barely came out on top in there scenario.

text:
Remember, folks: Manufacturers can set the sticker price of something at $1 or $1 billion; the market determines the actual price based on quality, utility and scarcity. If a good or service can be scalped, that means it was priced below the market to begin with. 
From a logical standpoint, if NVIDIA really wanted to make money, they'd sell all their cards through an official eBay account at auction.  Selling a good or service low only to have the scalpers profit off all your hard work and investment is cutting your own throat.

text: Huge mistake in the video RTX mega geometry is not meant to do tghe same job as nanite from Unreal Engine rather it's the equivalent of Nanite for specifically the BVH structure which is used for ray tracing, traditionally BVH have to be constantly rebuild and reloaded which is an intensive task, which when combined with every changing lods, or nanite where the geometry is changing constantly due to real lod construction, the BVH structures had to maintain a lower level of detail constantly due to how costly it is to rebuild them all of them if we want to ray trace against the highest level of detail geometry, so what RTX mega geometry allows is dynamic loading of polygon clusters into the BVH without having to do a full rebuild, allowing games to have higher level of detail ray tracing results with way loss cost due to the absence of all the BVH rebuilds we had to do without this feature, so it work harmoniously with stuff like nanite it doesn't replace it .....

text:
I reserved my judgement on the new 50 series, contrary to all the moaning from the internet brigade and remained optimistic until I started seeing the reviews, but that Black Myth Wukong 1440p RT performance across the board should be worrying to people, just on its own.

I mean, this is the 9th generation of gaming let's call it and this can't even run the latest game at 1440p with RT comfortably, so 2160p is really out of the question - NOT acceptable for a brand new $2,000 high end class graphics card!

I'm currently using an RTX 3080 and can honestly say that this card, for the relatively little that I paid for it, is holding up extremely well for my 4K gaming, I don't need everything turned up to max and don't need more than 60 frames (using 55" OLED TV).   The price to performance for this card continues to be outstanding, even if you paid full MSRP for it, the only card that had better value was the card I traded it in for, which was my GTX 1080 ti.

Not sure I can justify an upgrade right now unless:-

a)  A particular game I want demands it

and 

b) I can be 100% confident that the card is going to be able to handle these games comfortably at 4K and 60 fps maxed out for the next 3 years at least, otherwise what is the point of an upgrade?  May as well just keep my existing card and scale back some settings if absolutely necessary, because cards are becoming too expensive.

It looks like the 5090 is already going to be hanging on if the games get more demanding than Wukong, something has got to give somewhere, because this upscaling technology will be very situational (most games are developed with console in mind first) and will surely have limitations when it comes to generating these extra AI frames effectively?  I don't count these generated frames as giving us a true upgrade card, although the technology is certainly interesting down on paper.

That Cyberpunk read out is not that impressive for an upgrade at 2160p, it should be eeking out a minimum of 65-70 fps on the 1% lows and giving something like 80-85fps at the top end to be considered a decent upgrade over the RTX 4090 in my opinion.  Even then, it's still a ways off being considered a strong high end 4K card, as newer games will be even more demanding than Cyberpunk.  I recall Linus trying out an SLI 8K test a while back for Cyberpunk - we can forget gaming at this resolution for some time it seems.

Considering 4K has been out for 13 years now, this should by now be a proper 4K gaming card without the need for gimmicks.

That power draw as well , that's insane, need to hook your PC up to a power station, not a power supply module.

text:
A MUCH bigger deal needs to be made about the flaws of AI Frame Generation. Since input latency is still based on the real framerate without the AI frames, the entire advantage of higher frame rate is negated. It does not FEEL like a higher framerate, it only appears to be. This is a threat to the quality of the video game industry. 

I've tried Frame Gen but never use it because it feels so awful and DELAYED. So much of the point of striving for a higher frame rate is to see a frame with new information faster so you can react to the information faster. But since frame gen still has the same or potentially worse latency than running the game with no frame gen, there's no point. Can I even trust if the information in the AI frame is accurate? All the AI has to work with is motion data and information from the previous frames, if that data does not prepare the AI for something unexpected then that makes the latency of new information even worse. AI Frame Generation negates all of the benefits of higher framerate. Many people don't understand this, especially with Nvidia marketing making it seem like free frames and putting Frame Gen on the same graphs as no Frame Gen. I'm so frustrated because nobody else is pointing out the full extent of how useless this technology is. I worry that many gamers will just see a bigger framerate number and turn it on, but their gameplay will suffer because of the increased latency and they won't know why. I think you guys should make a video covering the problems with AI Frame Generation to spread awareness. I worry the industry will be forever tainted by poor optimization with AI Frame Generation slapped on as a band-aid fix. There are already so many very poorly optimized games releasing with DLSS as a band-aid fix for the poor performance. If this is not denounced it will only get more common and worse. 

TLDR: The latency problems that AI Frame Generation have negate the benefits of higher frame rate. It does not FEEL like a higher framerate, it only appears to be. The average consumer does not understand this. This poses a threat to the greater gaming industry, as AI Gen tech is already commonly used as a band-aid fix by game devs for poor game optimization. You guys should make a video to spread awareness to these issues.

to be completely honest, I see the 50 series generation to be the "productivity generation". The 30 and 40 series could be defined as the "true ray tracing" generation, while the 10 and 16 series felt like the "digital realism" generation. Especially since AI is a huge focus on the 50 series's capabilities and there are a lot of back end processes that show promise (aside from DLSS and MFG) that are in development, the 50 series could open up new doors on the developmental side of games.

This means we could hopefully see faster game releases, better data compression and data management (leading to more reasonable game sizes, faster load times, larger maps, etc.) and better game engine optimization. text:
Frame gen being accessible from a 3rd party software for similar performance and artifacting has completely trivialized latest gen hardware for me. I'm still rocking a 3080 10gb at 1080p and when I pump game settings on the latest titles to the max I can just about fill out the 144hz of my monitor on most and just barely pass 60 on the heavy hitters (with some settings adjustments).

Now instead if I lock my fps to 60 for those same titles and only use lossless scalings framegen tech, I can get as many frames as I want to fill in my 144hz monitor, or if I choose to upgrade, 240 or more (technically there's an infinite scaler and higher refresh monitors, but I like 120-144 monitors best). 

As long as my system can run the game natively at around 65-70 frames with whatever options I choose, frame gen is absolutely amazing to give my single player experience a competitive game like feel with extra smoothness

text: 18:14 notice that FP4 is actually slower on the RTX 4090 than FP8. FP4 is such a pointless exercise, it's useful to do fun test runs of models that are too large for your card, but using 4 bits (where one is the sign so effectively 3 bits) to represent a floating point number in a production AI model is so ludicrous that I can't even believe they'd bring it up as a major selling point. For comparison, a 4 bit signed integer would only be able to store and work with numbers in a range from -7 to +7. Whereas a 16 bit signed integer can work with numbers in a range from -32,768 to 32,767.

text:
I'm hoping to upgrade my 7 year old gaming rig in April this year. I have an R5 2600 and an RX590. I'm a little bit of an AMD fanboy, but I'm aware that being a "fan" is not intelligent. I hate NVIDIA, but this 50 series GPUs are looking mighty fine. If AMD doesn't come up with something at least similar to this by April, I might jump the ship and get an NVIDIA card.
Also, I've been living off of FSR3 and FSR3 FG these last couple of years to keep using my RX590 with my 3440x1440 144Hz monitor (I had originally bought my rig to play 1080p 60FPS) and, since I had a potato PC during my upbringing, I seriously can't be bothered to notice any of the "artifacts" and other crap that comes along with those technologies vs running native. I just play the games and enjoy them. I also play a lot with my Steam Deck, which is not the most powerful gaming machine, and also still enjoy my games. I don't play any multiplayer games though and I like more graphic details than FPS, so I'm ok with 30FPS gaming.

author: @Lead_Foot

text:
@agustinmorquecho7781  Ryuujinx is the most accurate of the two Switch emulators, so I think it wouldn't get over the intended maximum framerate (30 or 60, depending on the game) without some heavy tinkering on the emulator itself or modding the games individually.

But for the sake of argument, let's say you can get the games to run beyond their intended framerate, and that causes them to run faster. That's because the game's speed is tied to the framerate, a complication I wish had died back in the N64 days, but seems to be present today still.

That's where Frame Generation would solve your problem. Frame Generation works by inserting "fake frames" between real ones, frames created by essentially calculating the differences between this frame and the next one. 

Since those frames are created AFTER the game's calculations have been made, it doesn't affect the game's speed whatsoever. That's how I get Xenoblade X to run at 60fps without messing the cutscenes like the 60fps mod does (though it does cause screen tearing even with VSync on, could be because my monitor does not support Free Sync).

But if you are sensitive to input lag, you will find the frame generation to be a detriment, as the information you will have on screen (the extra frames) does not align with what has been actually calculated in-engine.

text:
Wouldn't it be better if the GPU rendered the game "without any graphics" (like just the meshes, engine, and physics things) and then used the "fake frames" to essentially colour these scenes in, the latency issue would go away? 

If you can get the GPU with AI elements to run at a Frame Gen Per Second (FGPS, lets makes it happen) of 200, running at a raster FPS of 50, why not render the FGPS at a base of 40 FPS, giving a FGPS of 120, and run the game engine without any rasterization at a higher FPS than the raster output as close to the FGPS as possible?

Hoping that makes some sort of sense, and that we see new engines developed to leverage this potential power sitting in the 5000 series.

TLDR; Could developers make an engine that runs at 4x the speed of the "fps output" of a games output to remove as much latency as possible. Generated frames would be overlaid with the actual input to output speed of the games engine

text:
TLDR;  looking into 5070 cuz frame gen not having latency is awesome for sorta free frames, and also curious about cpu performance with that many frames

honestly I have a 3080 and really thinking about looking into a 5070. I'm a cod player, and hearing that it won't add any latency is AMAZING to hear, with my 3080 I can run cod at 100fps (while streaming) and around 144-180 fps (cod is awefully optimized on warzone) while not streaming, the fact that the dlss is going to be better, the frame generation (which I use amd to do in some games and am 100% OK with the quality on screen but hate the delay) is going to be no cost at latency, this is AMAZING to hear. I'm so happy this is the case, in my eyes a little artifacting in literally any game is something I can get over as long as I get higher frames, and no hit in latency. I think if people stop being AS picky we could all agree that if you were ok with dlss 3.0 then dlss 4.0 with frame gen for 1-3x the frame rate and no crazy hit on standard frames and latency that we will end up all using it. text:
I think LTT would really benefit from hiring someone with actual machine learning expertise. These comments on anything AI related are just constantly off the mark.
"Quantization" is the process of transforming a neural network architecture to a lower precision number type. So less bits per weight/data used. If done cleverly you can keep accuracy high while massively reducing memory usage and number of FLOPS (calculations). This has gotten very popular in recent years to make large networks feasible and to improve efficiency in general. "For simpler AI models that don't require high precision" is complete nonsense.

text:
To be fair, with the size of the nodes approaching 1nm and the wafer cost of smaller node manufacturing,  its really not surprising. If youre spending 30k on a wafer that can make 30gpus vs spending 10k on one that can make 50, its obvious theres going to be price hikes.

This will likely be the shtick for awhile until paralell processing can be properly optimized. I think the future will have to move away from x86 architecture and dare i say...embrace ARM/GPU style multicores...but probably in a way i cant imagine...

But if i were to imagine,  it would look like gpus and cpus (APU) would esstentially be the same thing.  I big old chip with hundreds of thousands of cores. They could also keep the gpu and cpu separate for easy upgrading, but i doubt thats without performance and cost drawbacks.The problem is of course creating a programming language. 

If i can imagine what that would look like, its basically a language too advanced for people to do themselves and would require AI to rewrite what functions youd intend for it to do in conventional programming, then translate it entirely it into something different. I understand most programming languages kind of do that, but id say its more akin to writing a program that tells another program to write the program in a completely different way...

Long story short, PC requires a pretty big evolution in the not too distant future to really see it take off again.

text: The intel 14400 can play gta v at 1080p with more than 60fps. You don't even need a GPU anymore with older titles and chill games. You can build a whole system for $300 and less if already got a PSU or SSD. Spend ($120/1080gtx) or ($70/980gtx) or ($60/780gtx) or ($50/680gtx) if you really want to try newer titles or but I suggest getting two CPU's and a video capture device. It's much more fun tinkering without spending a whole year of your grocery bill with things like using two PC's in any game you want or setting one for recording gameplay or editing a video while you use the other. Having maxed out settings in a game is meh unless its 1: resolution (added detail to all textures, 2: vsync (smoothness in gameplay/no screen tearing) 3: motion blur (cinema/just straight up fun/making a game feel alive) > anti-aliasing/ray tracing/ect (stuff that cuts your fps in half, stay away from those completely or last if you will) id rather have 1440p or 2160p with vsync and motion blur on, everything else low before I decide what setting to add next would be, texture filtering/shaders/main texture/lighting and any other effect then lastly shadows, anti-aliasing and ray tracting for those have the most impact

RT is used by devs to introduce lighting much easier (and it can look great)but it's a new entire way of rendering thus it requires hardware that can do it and that's hard (see the FPS). RT is here to stay

text:
Casualmente son las mismas conclusiones a las que llegué luego de probar la GPU en el CES y que detalle a fondo en mi video de PC NOTICIAS: "No compres una RTX 50 sin antes ver este video"

Veamos:

-La 5090 es la GPU más potente de escritorio que existe hoy por hoy, sin discusión, tanto a nivel de rasterizado como a nivel de Ray tracing

-La 5090 es la GPU de escrito que más consume, sin discusión, en juegos llega a consumir más de 560W, eso es más de 100W por encima de la 4090

-La diferencia de rendimiento entre la 5090 a la 4090 es mucho más pequeña que de la 4090 a la 3090, es decir: hubo un salto más grande de potencia de la 4090 vs la 3090, que de la 5090 vs 4090

-La 5090 queda entre las tarjetas con relación precio/ desempeño menos favorable. Es la más potente y exclusiva y la exclusividad se paga

-La 5090 presenta las latencias más bajas al jugar usando reescalado (menos de 30ms) pero son las más altas al activar el multi frame generation (más de 50 ms)

-El reflex 2 para bajar latencias solamente estará disponible de momento en dos juegos, tocará esperar a que se implemente en más juegos y ver si vale la pena jugar con el MFG sin que el juego se sienta muy laggeado.

text: If someone uses the RT and Tensor cores for work purposes, this can make more sense than games-only, but even then I think it’s a hard sell unless there’s money to burn. For instance, ray tracing is still an amazing tech, but I consider it not at all worth the performance hit. Going to a 20-series card from my 1080, however, was giant in accelerating certain tasks I do — video editing encoding / acceleration, some AI tools in such softwares, and way faster map baking in programs like Substance. The GPU light mass in Unreal Engine also requires an RTX-level card, and is VASTLY faster than CPU-based equivalents. Then there’s GPU rendering for 3D apps (like Redshift, Octane Render, etc) that are massively accelerated with the tensor cores & tech. That being said…I won’t be getting this generation. I have a 1080 FE, and 2080 blower, and a 3080 blower in one PC. I LOVED the bower designs, as it let you stack your cards in one chassis. One day I’ll upgrade my entire PC (6700K still rocking!) and likely look at a new GPU then, but the new features on these cards are very likely to NOT do much with the majority of new games, since they require specific attention to the new tech.

​​​​​ @manuelsputnik  Rasterization is the benchmark if you're an old head that wants tech to be stuck in the same place forever. Raster performance is pretty much okay by now. Most cards can already get good FPS at its intended resolution. Getting more on top of that is just bonus.

RT and PT are fine and actually good innovation in tech. Yes, no GPU on earth can do 4k60 native with PATH tracing yet but that's not a reason to constantly whine and act like raster is all we will ever need. Real time path tracing was thought to be impossible for decades. Now you can get 30 FPS at 4k in a game as pretty and full of detail like Cyberpunk. People forget how many pixels need to be rendered in 4k and how heavy it is without PT. That's progress!

Yes, the 5090 is stupid expensive but that card is not what a normal gamer should get in the first place. It's a luxury halo product made to push the boundary of tech. It's like complaining that a Porsche or McLaren is too expensive for normal people. Well, duh. Their reason of existing is to enable development of new tech that will eventually arrive at lower price points.

As for it struggling at Wukong. If it can do well in Cyberpunk and so many other games that are arguably prettier than Wukong, it says more about how poorly optimized UE5 and Wukong are. That's a dev problem not a hardware problem. The devs need to optimize it instead of people saying that the 5090 is bad or something because it struggles with a poorly optimized game.

​ @nathanielhill8156  most standard circuits in NA are 15a at 120v, some circuits are 20a but generally used for small appliance circuits in kitchens as required by the NEC. No single item connected to a circuit should exceed 80% of the circuit rating so for 15a that's 1480w and 1800w for a 20a. Now you can load up a circuit but you have to understand how your circuits are laid out. Very rare for a room imo to only have one branch breaker feeding it.

Side note you can run a 240v circuit and then use an EU PSU. Voltage input ranges on power supply are usually safe up to 250v and will work at 60hz

Not recommending anyone do this but you could move your neutral to the opposite phases of the current hot using a 2 pole breaker and then make sure the plugs are rated for 240v. Again please don't do this but it's a quick way to make a 240v.

text: ​@ With Nvidia's built-in integer-scaling, the 1080 Ti at 4X integer with 25% of your monitor's native resolution being rendered, you can get a locked 240FPS with zero added latency and 90-95% of the fidelity is retained that you would get with a native resolution, integer-scaling is so underrated, zero added latency for 4X performance with almost no fidelity loss, so much better than the A.I. nonsense, I wouldn't be surprised if Nvidia removed integer-scaling as it's so much better than their DLSS, if they did that, I'd just use external hardware integer-scaling like the OSSC Pro or Tink4K, which have much more options and modes as well as being still zero added latency, the opposite is also really good, you can internally render old games with 8 or 16 times or whatever you like the native resolution, say 16K rendering mapped to 1440p or 4K using Nvidia DSR (a native rendering method, so no A.I.), and this doesn't add any latency either, can make older games look incredible on a nice OLED monitor, better than most remasters imo.
